'''William Ball Provine''' (February 19, 1942 – September 1, 2015)<ref name="Cornell Obit" /> was an American [[History of science|historian of science]] and of [[evolutionary biology]] and [[population genetics]]. He was the Andrew H. and James S. Tisch Distinguished University Professor at [[Cornell University]] and was a professor in the [[Cornell University Department of History|Departments of History, Science and Technology Studies, and Ecology and Evolutionary Biology]].

==Biography==

Provine was born in [[Tennessee]]. He held a B.S. in mathematics (1962), and an M.A. (1965) and Ph.D. (1970) in the [[history of science]] from the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="Provine VIVO">{{cite web
|url=https://vivo.cornell.edu/display/individual5223
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141031031538/http://vivo.cornell.edu/display/individual5223
|url-status=dead
|archive-date=October 31, 2014
|title=Provine, William Ball
|work=VIVO}}</ref> He joined the Cornell faculty in 1969. He suffered seizures in 1995 due to a brain tumour.<ref name="No Free Will">{{cite journal
|last=Provine |first=Will
|year=1999 |volume=90 |pages=S117–32
|publisher=University of Chicago Press, History of Science Society
|title=No Free Will
|journal=Isis |issn=0021-1753 |doi=10.1086/384611 |jstor=238010|s2cid=144040851
}}</ref> Provine died on September 1, 2015, due to complications from the tumor.<ref name="Cornell Obit">{{cite news
|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2015/09/william-provine-history-science-scholar-dies-73
|first=Krishna |last=Ramanujan
|title=William Provine, History of Science Scholar, Dies at 73
|work=Cornell Chronicle
|date=September 9, 2015}}</ref>

==History of theoretical population genetics==

Provine's Ph.D. thesis, later published as a book,<ref>{{cite book|last=Provine|first=William B.|title=The Origins of Theoretical Population Genetics|date=1971|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=0-226-68465-2|url=https://archive.org/details/originsoftheoret00prov}}</ref> documented the early origins of theoretical population genetics in the conflicts between the [[biostatistics]] and [[Gregor Mendel|Mendelian]] schools of thought. He documented later developments in theoretical population genetics in his biography of [[Sewall Wright]],<ref>{{cite book|last=Provine|first=William B.|title=Sewall Wright and Evolutionary Biology|date=1989|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=0-226-68473-3|edition=Pbk.|url=https://archive.org/details/sewallwrightevol00will}}</ref> who was still alive and available for interviews. In this book, Provine criticizes Wright for confounding three different concepts of [[adaptive landscape]]: genotype to fitness landscapes, allele frequency to fitness landscapes, and phenotype to fitness landscapes. Provine later grew critical of Wright's views on [[genetic drift]], instead attributing observed effects to the consequences of inbreeding and consequent selection at linked sites. [[John H. Gillespie]] credits Provine with stimulating his interest in the topic of [[genetic hitchhiking|hitchhiking or "genetic draft"]] as an alternative to genetic drift.<ref>{{cite journal
|last=Gillespie|first=J. H.
|title=Is the Population Size of a Species Relevant to its Evolution?
|journal=Evolution
|date=11 November 2001|volume=55|issue=11|pages=2161–69|pmid=11794777|doi=10.1554/0014-3820(2001)055[2161:itpsoa]2.0.co;2}}</ref> Provine later published his critique of genetic drift in a book.<ref>{{cite book
|last=Provine|first=William B.
|title=The "Random Genetic Drift" Fallacy
|date= 2014 |isbn=9781500924126

|publisher=CreateSpace}}</ref> Provine defended the importance of mathematics' contribution to the [[modern synthesis (20th century)|modern evolutionary synthesis]].<ref>{{cite journal
|last=Provine|first=William B.
|title=The Role of Mathematical Population Geneticists in the Evolutionary Synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s
|journal=Studies in the History of Biology|date=1978|volume=2|pages=167–92|pmid=11610409
}}</ref>

==Education reform==
In 1970, Provine was instrumental in the founding of Cornell's [[Risley Residential College]]. He was the first faculty member in residence.

==Philosophy==

Provine was a philosopher, [[Atheism|atheist]], and critic of [[intelligent design]]. He engaged in prominent debates with theist philosophers and scientists about the existence of God and the viability of intelligent design. He debated the founder of the [[intelligent design movement]], [[Phillip E. Johnson]], and the two had a friendly relationship. Provine said that his course on evolutionary biology began by having his students read Johnson's book, ''[[Darwin on Trial]]''.<ref name="Que Res Vitas">{{cite journal
|url=http://www.arn.org/docs/orpages/or161/pjlect.htm
|first=John Mark |last=Reynolds
|title=Que Res Vitas?: Phil Johnson Takes His Case to the East
|journal=Origins Research
|volume=16  |number=1  |date=June 2, 1995
|publisher=[[Access Research Network]]}}</ref>

Provine was a [[Determinism|determinist]], as he rejected the idea that humans exercise [[free will]].<ref name="No Free Will"/><ref name="Free Will and Punishment">{{cite web
|last=Provine|first=William|title=Evolution: Free Will and Punishment and Meaning in Life
|date=February 12, 1998
|url=http://eeb.bio.utk.edu/darwin/Archives/1998ProvineAbstract.htm |url-status=dead
|work=Second Annual Darwin Day Celebration |publisher=University of Tennessee, Knoxville
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070829083051/http://eeb.bio.utk.edu/darwin/Archives/1998ProvineAbstract.htm
|archive-date=August 29, 2007 |access-date=October 30, 2015}}</ref> Provine asserted that there is no evidence for the existence of [[God]], no [[Afterlife|life after death]], no absolute foundation for moral right and wrong, and no ultimate meaning or purpose for life. He was once a [[Presbyterian]] like his friend and intellectual rival Johnson, saying their worldviews had been much the same before he became an atheist.<ref name="Provine-Johnson Apr 1994 Debate">{{cite journal
|url=http://www.arn.org/docs/orpages/or161/161main.htm
|title=Darwinism: Science or Naturalistic Philosophy?, A Debate Between William B. Provine and Phillip E. Johnson at Stanford University, April 30, 1994
|first1=William B. |last1=Provine |first2=Phillip E. |last2=Johnson
|journal=Origins Research
|volume=16  |number=1  |date=June 2, 1995
|publisher=Access Research Network}} Video at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m7dG9U1vQ_U.</ref>

==In popular culture==
Professor Provine appeared in [[Ben Stein]]'s movie ''[[Expelled: No Intelligence Allowed]]''. Provine supervised the doctoral dissertation written by [[Bad Religion]] member [[Greg Graffin]]. Graffin was a student of history of science at Cornell. Provine also supervised [[Steve Leveen]]'s sociology dissertation in 1982.
